binders: In the first conjunct: for every type Omega in any universe, every measurable-space structure on Omega, every measure mu on Omega that is a probability measure, and every function X : Omega -> Real.
Inside the boundedness hypothesis: there exists one real constant C such that the bound holds for every omega in Omega.
In each of the last two conjuncts: for every real lambda.
hypotheses: For the first conjunct, X is measurable.
For the first conjunct, X is uniformly bounded: there exists a real C such that |X(omega)| <= C for every omega.
For the first conjunct, the integral of X with respect to mu is 0.
For the first conjunct, the integral of X(omega)^2 with respect to mu is 1.
For the exponential-measure finite-integral branch, lambda < 1.
For the exponential-measure nonintegrability branch, 1 <= lambda.
conclusions: As lambda approaches 0, integral exp(lambda X(omega)) dmu(omega) - 1 - lambda integral X dmu - (lambda^2/2) integral X^2 dmu is o(lambda^2).
As lambda approaches 0, exp(lambda^2/2) - (1 + lambda^2/2) is o(lambda^2).
For every real lambda < 1, x mapped to exp(lambda x) is integrable with respect to the unit-parameter exponential measure, and its integral equals 1/(1-lambda).
For every real lambda >= 1, x mapped to exp(lambda x) is not integrable with respect to the unit-parameter exponential measure.
mathematical_definitions: The little-o relations are normed asymptotic relations along the usual real neighborhood filter at 0.
The integrals are real-valued Bochner integrals.
The fixed measure expMeasure(1) is defined in the dossier as gammaMeasure(1, 1), i.e. the unit-parameter exponential measure.
Real absolute value is max(x,-x), and the norm on Real is absolute value.
Integrable means almost-everywhere strongly measurable and having finite integral norm.
translation.proposition_plain_english: All of the following hold simultaneously. First, every bounded measurable real random variable X on an arbitrary probability space, if centered and with second moment one, has the second-order moment-generating-function expansion E[exp(lambda X)] = 1 + lambda E[X] + (lambda^2/2)E[X^2] + o(lambda^2) as lambda tends to zero. Second, exp(lambda^2/2) = 1 + lambda^2/2 + o(lambda^2) as lambda tends to zero. Third, under the unit-parameter exponential measure, exp(lambda x) is integrable exactly for lambda < 1: in that regime its integral is 1/(1-lambda), while for lambda >= 1 it is not integrable.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The first expansion is restricted to real-valued X that are measurable, uniformly pointwise bounded, centered, and have second moment exactly one, on a probability measure over an otherwise arbitrary measurable type.

The bound is pointwise for every omega, not merely almost everywhere; C is existentially quantified and is not explicitly required to be nonnegative, although existence of the stated bound on a probability space forces an adequate bound.
The little-o conclusions are only local as lambda approaches zero; no quantitative neighborhood, rate, or global inequality is encoded.
The target explicitly subtracts lambda times the first moment and (lambda^2/2) times the second moment even though the hypotheses fix those moments to 0 and 1.
The last two clauses cover all real lambda using the split lambda < 1 versus lambda >= 1, including the boundary lambda = 1 in the nonintegrable regime.
No support description, density formula, or probabilistic random-variable realization of expMeasure(1) is encoded directly; only its definition as gammaMeasure(1,1) appears in the dossier.

Because Lean's integral operator is total even outside the integrable case, its behavior for nonintegrable functions could matter in other statements; here the equality branch also explicitly asserts integrability.
ambiguities: The one-level definition bodies supplied for Asymptotics.IsLittleO, MeasureTheory.integral, and nhds are opaque wrappers, so their standard mathematical readings as little-o, Bochner integral, and neighborhood filter are not independently recoverable from those bodies alone.

The dossier defines expMeasure(r) as gammaMeasure(1,r) but does not expose gammaMeasure's definition, so the description 'unit-parameter exponential measure' relies on the provided declaration name and parameterization rather than a displayed density.
